issue.issue_text: Whether the offence of forgery under Section 464 of the Indian Penal Code is made out when the essential requirement of making a 'false document' as per Explanation 2 of the section is not satisfied.

facts: Accused no. 1, with the assistance of an imposter impersonating a property owner, created a Power of Attorney (PoA) in his own name.
Using this fraudulent PoA, accused no. 1 executed a mortgage deed for the property in favor of accused no. 2.
The trial court and Sessions court convicted the accused, but the High Court acquitted them, finding that the requirements for forgery were not met.
law: Section 463 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) defines the offense of forgery.
Section 464 IPC explains what constitutes 'making a false document', which is a necessary ingredient for the offense of forgery.
To convict someone for forgery under Section 465 IPC, the prosecution must first prove that forgery was committed under Section 463, which requires satisfying the conditions of Section 464.
Explanation 2 to Section 464 clarifies that for an offense of forgery, it is imperative that a false document is made and that the accused person is the 'maker' of that document.
The court distinguishes between 'making' a document and 'causing it to be made'. Forgery can only be imposed on the person who is the actual maker.
application: The Court determined that the 'maker' of the false document (the Power of Attorney) was the imposter who impersonated the owner and signed it.
There was no finding by the lower courts that the accused-respondents themselves had actually made or signed the false document.
While the accused were the beneficiaries and caused the document to be made, they did not fit the legal definition of being the 'maker'.
Since the accused were not the makers of the forged document, the essential requirement of Section 464 was not satisfied against them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the charge of forgery, holding that the offense is not made out if the accused is not the 'maker' of the false document. Because the imposter, not the accused, created the fraudulent Power of Attorney, a crucial ingredient of Section 464 was not met, and therefore, the accused could not be held liable for forgery.

issue.issue_text: Whether the offence of cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code can be sustained when it is consequential to the primary offence of forgery under Section 464, which itself is not established.

facts: An imposter, impersonating a property owner, created a fraudulent Power of Attorney (PoA) in the name of accused no. 1.
Using this fraudulent PoA, accused no. 1 executed a mortgage deed for the property in favor of accused no. 2.
The High Court acquitted the accused, overturning their convictions from the lower courts.
law: The offence of forgery is defined in Section 463 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), and a key ingredient is the 'making of a false document' as explained in Section 464.
According to Explanation 2 of Section 464, to be liable for forgery, the accused person must be the actual 'maker' of the false document.
The act of 'making' a false document is distinct from 'causing it to be made'.
In this case, the offence of cheating under Section 420 was considered consequential to the primary offence of forgery.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the accused-respondents were not the 'makers' of the forged Power of Attorney; the imposter was.
The prosecution failed to provide evidence proving that the respondents themselves had created the false document.
Since the essential ingredient of 'making a false document' under Section 464 was not established against the accused, the charge of forgery could not be sustained.
The Court agreed with the High Court's reasoning that because the primary offence of forgery failed, the consequential charge of cheating under Section 420 must also fail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, holding that a charge of cheating under Section 420 cannot be sustained when it is dependent on a primary charge of forgery, and the prosecution has failed to prove that the accused actually made the false document as required by Section 464 of the IPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A document, even if created dishonestly or fraudulently, is not considered a "false document" for the purposes of forgery unless it is made with the specific intention of causing it to be believed that it was made by, or under the authority of, a person by whom it was not actually made.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the conviction for forgery could not be sustained because the prosecution failed to prove the essential elements of the offence. The case was based on suspicion and the fact that the accused was a beneficiary, which cannot substitute for legal proof. The investigation was lopsided and failed to establish that the initial Power of Attorney was a fraudulent transaction, and the act itself did not meet the definition of making a 'false document' under Section 464 of the IPC.
legal_tests_applied: The test for what constitutes a 'false document' under Section 464 IPC, which requires one of three conditions to be met: 1) making a document with the intent to make it seem it was made by someone else; 2) altering a document without lawful authority after it has been made; or 3) causing a person without mental capacity (due to intoxication, etc.) to sign a document without knowing its contents.

The evidence did not meet the criteria for making a 'false document' under Section 464, as the document was not made to appear as if it was made by someone else, was not altered, and was not signed by someone lacking mental capacity.
The case rested on suspicion and the accused being a beneficiary, which the court held cannot take the place of legal proof.

policy_considerations: A duty is cast upon the courts to ensure that suspicion does not take place of the legal proof.
Strong suspicion, coincidence, grave doubt cannot take the place of proof.

If this is the coordination between the prosecution and the investigating agency, every criminal case tend to end up in acquittal. In the process, the common man will lose confidence on the criminal justice delivery system, which is not a good symptom.
It is the duty of the investigation, prosecution as well as the Courts to ensure that full and material facts and evidence are brought on record, so that there is no scope for miscarriage of justice.
